topics.title: Myths retold: Persephone, Orpheus and Arachne
topics.intro: Greek myths explain the world (why winter comes, where spiders came from) and test human beings against the gods. Read each one closely: who breaks a rule, and what does it cost them?
topics.teach: Explain how the Persephone myth explains the seasons.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which myth {she} would retell in a modern setting, and how.
topics.hook: Every myth asks the same two questions: who broke the rule, and what did it cost them?

topics.title: Homer: Hector and the Sirens
topics.intro: The Iliad and the Odyssey are nearly 3,000 years old and are the oldest stories in Western literature. One extract is in prose; the other is in rhyming couplets, as Alexander Pope translated it in the 1720s.
topics.teach: Explain why Hector takes off his helmet, and what that moment shows about him.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether Odysseus was brave or just clever to have himself tied to the mast.
topics.hook: The **Iliad** is named after Ilion, the Greek name for Troy; the **Odyssey** after Odysseus, who takes ten years to get home.

topics.title: How great novels begin
topics.intro: A first page has to hook the reader, set up the world and hint at what is to come. Dickens and Austen begin with two of the most famous sentences in English, and both are being slyly ironic.
topics.teach: Explain why Austen’s first sentence is ironic.
topics.talk: Read the first lines of the book {she} is reading now together. What do they promise?
topics.hook: A great first line is a promise: it hooks the reader and hints at the whole book.

topics.title: Gothic horror: Frankenstein and Jekyll
topics.intro: Gothic fiction is about fear: dark nights, secret experiments, the monster that may be inside us. Notice how both writers make the reader wait for the horror and how they describe it.
topics.teach: Explain why Victor runs away from the creature he has worked so hard to make.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what makes something frightening on the page rather than on screen.
topics.hook: Gothic = fear in the dark: a lonely setting, a secret, and a monster who might be one of us.

topics.title: Detective fiction: Sherlock Holmes
topics.intro: Detective stories are built on inference: clues, deductions, and a narrator who sees less than the detective. Read Watson’s reasoning carefully. Is he as clever as he thinks?
topics.teach: Explain the difference between an observation and a deduction.
topics.talk: Play a game of deductions: what can you infer about a stranger from their shoes?
topics.hook: Observe, then deduce: what you see is the clue; what you work out from it is the answer.

topics.title: Character and setting: Miss Havisham
topics.intro: Dickens builds one of the strangest characters in fiction from objects: a dress, a shoe, a veil. As you read, ask what each detail suggests about her past.
topics.teach: Explain how Dickens uses the colour white in this extract.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what Miss Havisham’s room says about her, and what {her} own room would say about {him}.
topics.hook: Stopped clocks, one shoe, a rotting wedding cake: Miss Havisham is a woman frozen at one moment.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Caliban in The Tempest
topics.intro: The Tempest was one of Shakespeare’s last plays. Caliban is called a monster by the other characters, yet he speaks some of the most beautiful poetry in the play. Read his two speeches aloud.
topics.teach: Explain why some readers feel sympathy for Caliban.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether Caliban is a villain or a victim, and why.
topics.hook: Caliban: called a monster, yet given some of the most beautiful lines in the play.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Macbeth’s dagger
topics.intro: A soliloquy lets the audience hear a character think. Macbeth is about to murder his king, and his mind is playing tricks on him. Read it aloud and listen for where the rhythm breaks.
topics.teach: Explain what the dagger soliloquy reveals about Macbeth’s state of mind.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether the dagger is real, a hallucination, or a sign from the witches.
topics.hook: Actors avoid saying the name inside a theatre and call it “the Scottish Play”.

topics.title: War poetry: Wilfred Owen
topics.intro: Wilfred Owen wrote about the First World War from inside it. His poems are angry and tender at once. “Anthem for Doomed Youth” is a sonnet that asks what funeral rites these soldiers will have.
topics.teach: Explain the contrast between the two halves of “Anthem for Doomed Youth”.
topics.talk: On Remembrance Sunday, read the poem aloud together.
topics.hook: Owen wrote that his subject was “War, and the pity of War”.

topics.title: Victorian poetry: the passing of Arthur
topics.intro: Tennyson was Queen Victoria’s Poet Laureate. Here he retells the end of King Arthur in blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter that sound like grand, heightened speech.
topics.teach: Explain how Tennyson makes the moment the sword is thrown feel magical.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Bedivere might not have wanted to throw such a beautiful sword away.
topics.hook: Blank verse: no rhyme, but the heartbeat stays, da-DUM five times a line.

topics.title: The craft of the short story
topics.intro: A short story has no room to waste. Every detail should matter, and the best ones plant clues that only make sense at the end. Read this story twice: once for the plot, once for the clues.
topics.teach: Explain how the writer foreshadows who the guard really is.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to plan a short story with a twist in five sentences.
topics.hook: In a short story nothing is wasted: every clue is planted to pay off at the end.

topics.title: The literature toolkit
topics.intro: The right term lets you say precisely what a writer is doing, which is the difference between a good answer and a top one.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between dramatic irony and foreshadowing.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to spot one technique in a song lyric.
topics.hook: Name it, quote it, explain it: the right term is the key that opens up the analysis.

topics.title: Writers and their worlds
topics.intro: Context means the world a text was written in. Knowing it helps you understand why a writer chose what they did, but always use it to explain the text, not instead of it.
topics.teach: Explain how knowing that Owen was a soldier changes how you read his poems.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which writer {she} would most like to interview, and what {she} would ask.
topics.hook: Context explains the text; it never replaces it.

topics.title: Greek tragedy and the epic
topics.intro: The Greeks invented tragedy and named its parts: the hero’s fatal flaw, the chorus, the reversal of fortune. Shakespeare, and every crime drama on television, still use their ideas.
topics.teach: Explain what hubris and hamartia mean, using a myth as an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which modern film follows the shape of a Greek tragedy.
topics.hook: Pride comes before a fall: hubris, then nemesis. That is the shape of a Greek tragedy.

topics.title: The Shakespearean sonnet: Romeo and Juliet
topics.intro: The play opens with a sonnet that gives away the ending. GCSE examiners love form: how a poem’s shape and rhyme carry its meaning.
topics.teach: Explain why Shakespeare tells the audience the ending before the play starts.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what changes when you know how a story ends.
topics.hook: Shakespearean sonnet: three quatrains and a couplet, 4 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 14 lines.

topics.title: GCSE poetry: Owen’s “Exposure”
topics.intro: “Exposure” is on many GCSE courses. Owen’s enemy here is not the other army but the weather, and the poem’s sounds, half-rhymes and refrain make the waiting unbearable.
topics.teach: Explain the effect of the repeated line “But nothing happens.”
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the soldiers are waiting for, and why that is worse than fighting.
topics.hook: “But nothing happens”: the refrain is the waiting itself, repeated until it hurts.

topics.title: Comparing texts
topics.intro: Comparison is a GCSE skill: find what two texts share, then explore how they differ. Use comparative connectives such as “whereas”, “similarly” and “in contrast”.
topics.teach: Explain one similarity and one difference between Hector and Owen’s soldiers.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to compare two films with the same story.
topics.hook: Compare = similar AND different. Link every point to both texts: whereas, similarly, in contrast.

items.passage:
Persephone and the Six Seeds

Persephone was gathering narcissus flowers in a meadow when the ground split open. Out of the dark came a chariot pulled by black horses, and in it stood Hades, lord of the dead. Before she could scream for her mother, he had swept her down into the Underworld, and the earth closed over them like a mouth.

Her mother was Demeter, goddess of the harvest. She searched for nine days without eating or sleeping, carrying a torch through every valley. When at last the Sun, who sees everything, told her the truth, her grief turned to fury. She left Olympus and walked the earth disguised as an old woman, and wherever she went, nothing grew. Wheat withered in the fields. Fruit shrivelled on the branch. People began to starve, and the gods, who loved the smoke of their offerings, grew afraid.

Zeus sent Hermes down to bring Persephone home. Hades did not argue. He only smiled, and offered her a pomegranate before she left. She had eaten nothing in the Underworld, but the journey was long, and the seeds glowed like rubies. She ate six.

Those six seeds bound her. Anyone who eats the food of the dead must return to them. So it was agreed: for six months of every year Persephone lives with her mother, and the world blossoms; for six months she sits beside Hades as queen of the Underworld, and Demeter mourns, and the fields lie bare beneath the frost.

That, the Greeks said, is why we have winter.

items.passage:
Orpheus Looks Back

When Orpheus played his lyre, rivers paused to listen and wild animals lay down at his feet. When his wife Eurydice died from a snake bite soon after their wedding, he did what no living man had dared: he walked down into the Underworld to fetch her back.

He played for Charon, the ferryman, who carried him across the river for nothing. He played for Cerberus, the three-headed dog, and all three heads fell asleep. At last he stood before Hades and Persephone and sang of his loss, and for the first and only time, tears ran down the iron cheeks of the king of the dead.

“Take her,” said Hades. “She will follow you up to the light. But you must not look back at her, not once, until you are both in the world above.”

So Orpheus climbed. The path was steep and silent. He could hear his own breathing, but not hers; he could hear his own footsteps, but not hers. Was she there? Had he been tricked? The doubt grew heavier with every step, until, with the sunlight already shining on his face, he could bear it no longer.

He turned.

Eurydice was there, one step behind him, still in the shadow. She reached out her hand, and as he reached for it she faded like mist, whispering a last farewell that he could barely hear.

Orpheus never played a happy song again.

items.passage:
Arachne’s Tapestry

In a small town in Lydia lived a girl called Arachne, the finest weaver in the world. People travelled for days to watch her fingers fly across the loom. “Surely,” they said, “the goddess Athena herself taught you.”

“No one taught me,” said Arachne. “I am better than Athena. Let her come and prove otherwise.”

Athena came, disguised as an old woman, and gently warned her to ask the goddess’s forgiveness. Arachne laughed in her face. So the old woman threw off her disguise, and there stood Athena, grey-eyed and tall, and the contest began.

Athena wove the gods of Olympus in their glory, and in each corner she showed a mortal who had challenged the gods and been punished. It was a warning, woven in thread.

Arachne ignored it. She wove the gods at their worst: tricking, lying, chasing and quarrelling. Her work was so perfect that the figures seemed to breathe. Even Athena could find no fault in it, and that, more than the insult, was what she could not bear. She tore the tapestry to pieces and struck Arachne with her shuttle.

Arachne’s body began to shrink. Her hair fell away. Her fingers grew long and thin and became legs, and her body became small and round. Athena had turned her into the first spider.

“Live, then,” said the goddess, “and weave for ever.”

And Arachne does. Look in any corner.

A quotation about what he can and cannot hear

Orpheus Looks Back

When Orpheus played his lyre, rivers paused to listen and wild animals lay down at his feet. When his wife Eurydice died from a snake bite soon after their wedding, he did what no living man had dared: he walked down into the Underworld to fetch her back.

He played for Charon, the ferryman, who carried him across the river for nothing. He played for Cerberus, the three-headed dog, and all three heads fell asleep. At last he stood before Hades and Persephone and sang of his loss, and for the first and only time, tears ran down the iron cheeks of the king of the dead.

“Take her,” said Hades. “She will follow you up to the light. But you must not look back at her, not once, until you are both in the world above.”

So Orpheus climbed. The path was steep and silent. He could hear his own breathing, but not hers; he could hear his own footsteps, but not hers. Was she there? Had he been tricked? The doubt grew heavier with every step, until, with the sunlight already shining on his face, he could bear it no longer.

He turned.

Eurydice was there, one step behind him, still in the shadow. She reached out her hand, and as he reached for it she faded like mist, whispering a last farewell that he could barely hear.

Orpheus never played a happy song again.

(Troy is under siege by the Greeks (the Achaeans). The Trojan prince Hector has come back from the battle and meets his wife, Andromache, on the city wall.)

Hector smiled as he looked upon the boy, but he did not speak, and Andromache stood by him weeping and taking his hand in her own. “Dear husband,” said she, “your valour will bring you to destruction; think on your infant son, and on my hapless self who ere long shall be your widow—for the Achaeans will set upon you in a body and kill you. It would be better for me, should I lose you, to lie dead and buried, for I shall have nothing left to comfort me when you are gone, save only sorrow. I have neither father nor mother now.

[…]

And Hector answered, “Wife, I too have thought upon all this, but with what face should I look upon the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked battle like a coward? I cannot do so: I know nothing save to fight bravely in the forefront of the Trojan host and win renown alike for my father and myself.

[…]

He stretched his arms towards his child, but the boy cried and nestled in his nurse’s bosom, scared at the sight of his father’s armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet. His father and mother laughed to see him, but Hector took the helmet from his head and laid it all gleaming upon the ground. Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms, praying over him the while to Jove and to all the gods. “Jove,” he cried, “grant that this my child may be even as myself, chief among the Trojans; let him be not less excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilius with his might. Then may one say of him as he comes from battle, ‘The son is far better than the father.’ May he bring back the blood-stained spoils of him whom he has laid low, and let his mother’s heart be glad.”

items.passage:
(Ulysses (the Roman name for Odysseus) is telling the story of his voyage home. The goddess Circe has warned him that the Sirens’ song lures sailors to their deaths.)

“While yet I speak the winged galley flies,
And lo! the Siren shores like mists arise.
Sunk were at once the winds; the air above,
And waves below, at once forgot to move;
Some demon calm’d the air and smooth’d the deep,
Hush’d the loud winds, and charm’d the waves to sleep.
Now every sail we furl, each oar we ply;
Lash’d by the stroke, the frothy waters fly.
The ductile wax with busy hands I mould,
And cleft in fragments, and the fragments roll’d;
The aerial region now grew warm with day,
The wax dissolved beneath the burning ray;
Then every ear I barr’d against the strain,
And from access of frenzy lock’d the brain.
Now round the masts my mates the fetters roll’d,
And bound me limb by limb with fold on fold.
Then bending to the stroke, the active train
Plunge all at once their oars, and cleave the main.

“While to the shore the rapid vessel flies,
Our swift approach the Siren choir descries;
Celestial music warbles from their tongue,
And thus the sweet deluders tune the song:

“‘Oh stay, O pride of Greece! Ulysses, stay!
Oh cease thy course, and listen to our lay!
Blest is the man ordain’d our voice to hear,
The song instructs the soul, and charms the ear.
Approach! thy soul shall into raptures rise!
Approach! and learn new wisdom from the wise!
We know whate’er the kings of mighty name
Achieved at Ilion in the field of fame;
Whate’er beneath the sun’s bright journey lies.
Oh stay, and learn new wisdom from the wise!’

“Thus the sweet charmers warbled o’er the main;
My soul takes wing to meet the heavenly strain;
I give the sign, and struggle to be free;
Swift row my mates, and shoot along the sea;
New chains they add, and rapid urge the way,
Till, dying off, the distant sounds decay;
Then scudding swiftly from the dangerous ground,
The deafen’d ear unlock’d, the chains unbound.

“While yet I speak the winged galley flies,
And lo! the Siren shores like mists arise.
Sunk were at once the winds; the air above,
And waves below, at once forgot to move;
Some demon calm’d the air and smooth’d the deep,
Hush’d the loud winds, and charm’d the waves to sleep.
Now every sail we furl, each oar we ply;
Lash’d by the stroke, the frothy waters fly.
The ductile wax with busy hands I mould,
And cleft in fragments, and the fragments roll’d;
The aerial region now grew warm with day,
The wax dissolved beneath the burning ray;
Then every ear I barr’d against the strain,
And from access of frenzy lock’d the brain.
Now round the masts my mates the fetters roll’d,
And bound me limb by limb with fold on fold.
Then bending to the stroke, the active train
Plunge all at once their oars, and cleave the main.

Our swift approach the Siren choir descries;
Celestial music warbles from their tongue,

Oh cease thy course, and listen to our lay!
Blest is the man ordain’d our voice to hear,

Approach! and learn new wisdom from the wise!

Achieved at Ilion in the field of fame;
Whate’er beneath the sun’s bright journey lies.

items.model: Homer presents Hector as a warrior who cannot escape his duty: he would be ashamed to face the Trojans “if I shirked battle like a coward”, and his helmet with its plume “that nodded fiercely” is a symbol of the violence of war. (The opening of the novel. Mr and Mrs Bennet have five unmarried daughters.)

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” said his lady to him one day, “have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?”

Mr. Bennet replied that he had not.

“But it is,” returned she; “for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it.”

Mr. Bennet made no answer.

“Do you not want to know who has taken it?” cried his wife impatiently.

“You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it.”

This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it, that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh! Single, my dear, to be sure! A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!”

“How so? How can it affect them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” replied his wife, “how can you be so tiresome! You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that his design in settling here?”

“Design! Nonsense, how can you talk so! But it is very likely that he may fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes.”

“I see no occasion for that. You and the girls may go, or you may send them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better, for as you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley may like you the best of the party.”

It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, I collected the instruments of life around me, that I might infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. It was already one in the morning; the rain pattered dismally against the panes, and my candle was nearly burnt out, when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.

How can I describe my emotions at this catastrophe, or how delineate the wretch whom with such infinite pains and care I had endeavoured to form? His limbs were in proportion, and I had selected his features as beautiful. Beautiful! Great God! His yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath; his hair was of a lustrous black, and flowing; his teeth of a pearly whiteness; but these luxuriances only formed a more horrid contrast with his watery eyes, that seemed almost of the same colour as the dun-white sockets in which they were set, his shrivelled complexion and straight black lips.

The different accidents of life are not so changeable as the feelings of human nature. I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body. For this I had deprived myself of rest and health. I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room and continued a long time traversing my bed-chamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep.

items.hook: Pathetic fallacy: the weather feels what the characters feel. Dreary night, dreadful deed.

(Mr Enfield is telling his cousin, the lawyer Mr Utterson, about something he saw outside a strange, shabby door in London.)

“Well, it was this way,” returned Mr. Enfield: “I was coming home from some place at the end of the world, about three o’clock of a black winter morning, and my way lay through a part of town where there was literally nothing to be seen but lamps. Street after street and all the folks asleep—street after street, all lighted up as if for a procession and all as empty as a church—till at last I got into that state of mind when a man listens and listens and begins to long for the sight of a policeman. All at once, I saw two figures: one a little man who was stumping along eastward at a good walk, and the other a girl of maybe eight or ten who was running as hard as she was able down a cross street. Well, sir, the two ran into one another naturally enough at the corner; and then came the horrible part of the thing; for the man trampled calmly over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground. It sounds nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man; it was like some damned Juggernaut. I gave a few halloa, took to my heels, collared my gentleman, and brought him back to where there was already quite a group about the screaming child. He was perfectly cool and made no resistance, but gave me one look, so ugly that it brought out the sweat on me like running. The people who had turned out were the girl’s own family; and pretty soon, the doctor, for whom she had been sent put in his appearance. Well, the child was not much the worse, more frightened, according to the Sawbones; and there you might have supposed would be an end to it.

items.prompt: Compare how Shelley and Stevenson make their “monsters” frightening. Use a quotation from each.
hints: Frankenstein: how the creature is described, and Victor’s reaction
Jekyll and Hyde: how the man behaves, and Enfield’s reaction
One similarity and one difference
Comparative connectives: similarly, whereas, in contrast
items.model: Both writers frighten the reader through the reactions of horrified witnesses, but they focus on different things. Shelley concentrates on the creature’s appearance: his “yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath”, so the horror is physical and Victor flees in “breathless horror and disgust”. Stevenson, in contrast, frightens us with behaviour: the man “trampled calmly over the child’s body”, and it is the word “calmly” that is chilling, because it suggests no conscience at all. Similarly, both monsters seem not quite human, a “wretch” in one and a “Juggernaut” in the other. Yet whereas Shelley makes us half pity her creature, Stevenson gives us nothing to pity.

items.passage:
(The narrator is Dr Watson, the friend and assistant of the detective Sherlock Holmes. A visitor has left his walking stick behind.)

Mr. Sherlock Holmes, who was usually very late in the mornings, save upon those not infrequent occasions when he was up all night, was seated at the breakfast table. I stood upon the hearth-rug and picked up the stick which our visitor had left behind him the night before. It was a fine, thick piece of wood, bulbous-headed, of the sort which is known as a “Penang lawyer.” Just under the head was a broad silver band nearly an inch across. “To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H.,” was engraved upon it, with the date “1884.” It was just such a stick as the old-fashioned family practitioner used to carry—dignified, solid, and reassuring.

“Well, Watson, what do you make of it?”

Holmes was sitting with his back to me, and I had given him no sign of my occupation.

“How did you know what I was doing? I believe you have eyes in the back of your head.”

“I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffee-pot in front of me,” said he. “But, tell me, Watson, what do you make of our visitor’s stick? Since we have been so unfortunate as to miss him and have no notion of his errand, this accidental souvenir becomes of importance. Let me hear you reconstruct the man by an examination of it.”

“I think,” said I, following as far as I could the methods of my companion, “that Dr. Mortimer is a successful, elderly medical man, well-esteemed since those who know him give him this mark of their appreciation.”

“Good!” said Holmes. “Excellent!”

“I think also that the probability is in favour of his being a country practitioner who does a great deal of his visiting on foot.”

“Why so?”

“Because this stick, though originally a very handsome one has been so knocked about that I can hardly imagine a town practitioner carrying it. The thick-iron ferrule is worn down, so it is evident that he has done a great amount of walking with it.”

“Perfectly sound!” said Holmes.

[…]

“Really, Watson, you excel yourself,” said Holmes, pushing back his chair and lighting a cigarette. “I am bound to say that in all the accounts which you have been so good as to give of my own small achievements you have habitually underrated your own abilities. It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you are a conductor of light.
items.passageSource: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Hound of the Baskervilles (1902)
items.hook: Holmes’s method: notice what everyone else overlooks, even a shiny coffee-pot.

items.passage:
(Pip, a poor village boy, has been sent to play at the house of the rich and mysterious Miss Havisham.)

She was dressed in rich materials,—satins, and lace, and silks,—all of white. Her shoes were white. And she had a long white veil dependent from her hair, and she had bridal flowers in her hair, but her hair was white. Some bright jewels sparkled on her neck and on her hands, and some other jewels lay sparkling on the table. Dresses, less splendid than the dress she wore, and half-packed trunks, were scattered about. She had not quite finished dressing, for she had but one shoe on,—the other was on the table near her hand,—her veil was but half arranged, her watch and chain were not put on, and some lace for her bosom lay with those trinkets, and with her handkerchief, and gloves, and some flowers, and a Prayer-Book all confusedly heaped about the looking-glass.

It was not in the first few moments that I saw all these things, though I saw more of them in the first moments than might be supposed. But I saw that everything within my view which ought to be white, had been white long ago, and had lost its lustre and was faded and yellow. I saw that the bride within the bridal dress had withered like the dress, and like the flowers, and had no brightness left but the brightness of her sunken eyes. I saw that the dress had been put upon the rounded figure of a young woman, and that the figure upon which it now hung loose had shrunk to skin and bone. Once, I had been taken to see some ghastly waxwork at the Fair, representing I know not what impossible personage lying in state. Once, I had been taken to one of our old marsh churches to see a skeleton in the ashes of a rich dress that had been dug out of a vault under the church pavement. Now, waxwork and skeleton seemed to have dark eyes that moved and looked at me. I should have cried out, if I could.

(Prospero, a magician, has ruled the island for twelve years. Caliban, the son of the witch Sycorax, lived there before him and is now his servant.)

This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother,
Which thou tak’st from me. When thou cam’st first,
Thou strok’st me and made much of me; wouldst give me
Water with berries in’t; and teach me how
To name the bigger light, and how the less,
That burn by day and night: and then I lov’d thee,
And show’d thee all the qualities o’ th’ isle,
The fresh springs, brine-pits, barren place, and fertile.
Curs’d be I that did so! All the charms
Of Sycorax, toads, beetles, bats, light on you!
For I am all the subjects that you have,
Which first was mine own king; and here you sty me
In this hard rock, whiles you do keep from me
The rest o’ th’ island.

[…]

Be not afeard: the isle is full of noises,
Sounds, and sweet airs, that give delight, and hurt not.
Sometimes a thousand twangling instruments
Will hum about mine ears; and sometimes voices,
That, if I then had wak’d after long sleep,
Will make me sleep again: and then, in dreaming,
The clouds methought would open and show riches
Ready to drop upon me; that, when I wak’d,
I cried to dream again.

items.model: Caliban is presented as both, which is what makes him so interesting. His curses are vicious: he wishes “toads, beetles, bats” upon Prospero, and other characters call him a monster. Yet he also has a strong case as a victim. He says “This island’s mine”, and explains that he showed Prospero “all the qualities o’ th’ isle” in return for kindness, only to be kept “in this hard rock”. Most strikingly, Shakespeare gives him the gentle, musical speech “Be not afeard”, in which he “cried to dream again”. A true monster would not long for beauty like this, so the audience is pushed towards pity.

(Macbeth has decided to murder King Duncan, who is a guest in his castle tonight. He is alone, waiting for his wife’s signal.)

Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee:—
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.
Art thou not, fatal vision, sensible
To feeling as to sight? or art thou but
A dagger of the mind, a false creation,
Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?
I see thee yet, in form as palpable
As this which now I draw.
Thou marshall’st me the way that I was going;
And such an instrument I was to use.
Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest: I see thee still;
And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood,
Which was not so before.—There’s no such thing:
It is the bloody business which informs
Thus to mine eyes.

[…]

Thou sure and firm-set earth,
Hear not my steps, which way they walk, for fear
Thy very stones prate of my whereabout,
And take the present horror from the time,
Which now suits with it.—Whiles I threat, he lives;
Words to the heat of deeds too cold breath gives.

[A bell rings.]

I go, and it is done; the bell invites me.
Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell
That summons thee to heaven or to hell.

(Wilfred Owen fought as an officer in the First World War. He wrote this poem in 1917 and was killed in France a week before the war ended.)

What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles’ rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.
No mockeries for them; no prayers nor bells,
Nor any voice of mourning save the choirs,—
The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells;
And bugles calling for them from sad shires.

What candles may be held to speed them all?
Not in the hands of boys, but in their eyes
Shall shine the holy glimmers of goodbyes.
The pallor of girls’ brows shall be their pall;
Their flowers the tenderness of patient minds,
And each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds.

(King Arthur is dying after his last battle. Twice he has sent his knight Sir Bedivere to throw his sword into the lake, and twice Bedivere has hidden it instead. Arthur speaks first.)

But, if thou spare to fling Excalibur,
I will arise and slay thee with my hands.’

Then quickly rose Sir Bedivere, and ran,
And, leaping down the ridges lightly, plunged
Among the bulrush beds, and clutched the sword,
And strongly wheeled and threw it.  The great brand
Made lightnings in the splendour of the moon,
And flashing round and round, and whirled in an arch,
Shot like a streamer of the northern morn,
Seen where the moving isles of winter shock
By night, with noises of the Northern Sea.
So flashed and fell the brand Excalibur:
But ere he dipt the surface, rose an arm
Clothed in white samite, mystic, wonderful,
And caught him by the hilt, and brandished him
Three times, and drew him under in the mere.
And lightly went the other to the King.

Then spoke King Arthur, drawing thicker breath:
‘Now see I by thine eyes that this is done.
Speak out:  what is it thou hast heard, or seen?’

And answer made the bold Sir Bedivere:
‘Sir King, I closed mine eyelids, lest the gems
Should blind my purpose, for I never saw,
Nor shall see, here or elsewhere, till I die,
Not though I live three lives of mortal men,
So great a miracle as yonder hilt.

items.passage:
The Forty-Fifth Step

Mira counted the steps of the British Museum every time she came, and there were always forty-four. Today there were forty-five.

She stopped. Her brother Theo walked straight into her and dropped his sketchbook. Their friend Kit, who never noticed anything that was not on a screen, kept going until the shadow of the great columns swallowed him.

“There’s an extra step,” Mira said.

“There’s an extra sister,” said Theo, picking up his pencils. “One who counts things.”

Inside, the Greek galleries were cool and almost empty. A guard with silver hair and a grey cardigan sat beside the case of painted pots, reading a paperback so old its cover had worn white. She looked up as they passed, and Mira had the odd feeling of being weighed, like fruit on a market stall. On the guard’s collar was a small brooch: an owl.

The pot Mira loved best showed a woman at a loom. “Arachne,” said Kit, reading the label on his phone. “She beat Athena at weaving. Legend.”

“She didn’t beat her,” said the guard, without looking up. “She was punished for being proud. Different thing.” She turned a page. “Though, between you and me, her work was better.”

Kit laughed. Mira didn’t. The guard’s eyes were grey, the clear, cold grey of a winter sea, and they were looking at Mira now.

“You count things,” said the guard. “Good. Most people only look.”

When Mira glanced back from the doorway, the chair was empty. The paperback lay closed on the seat.

Outside, the light was already fading. Mira counted the steps on the way down. Forty-four.

On the place where the forty-fifth had been lay a single grey feather.

items.passage:
(The Prologue is spoken by the Chorus before the play begins.)

Two households, both alike in dignity,
In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life;
Whose misadventur’d piteous overthrows
Doth with their death bury their parents’ strife.
The fearful passage of their death-mark’d love,
And the continuance of their parents’ rage,
Which but their children’s end naught could remove,
Is now the two hours’ traffic of our stage;
The which, if you with patient ears attend,
What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

items.model: Shakespeare uses the sonnet, the traditional form of love poetry, to tell us that this will be a love story, yet he fills it with violence. The “ancient grudge” breaks out in “new mutiny”, and the pun in “civil blood makes civil hands unclean” shows citizens destroying each other. The lovers are “star-cross’d” and their love is “death-mark’d”, so from the start the audience knows they are doomed by fate. This creates dramatic irony that hangs over every happy scene: we watch knowing that only “their children’s end” will end their parents’ rage.

items.passage:
(Owen describes soldiers waiting through a freezing night in the trenches in the winter of 1917.)

Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knife us . . .
Wearied we keep awake because the night is silent . . .
Low drooping flares confuse our memory of the salient . . .
Worried by silence, sentries whisper, curious, nervous,
But nothing happens.

Watching, we hear the mad gusts tugging on the wire,
Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles.
Northward incessantly, the flickering gunnery rumbles,
Far off, like a dull rumour of some other war.
What are we doing here?

The poignant misery of dawn begins to grow . . .
We only know war lasts, rain soaks, and clouds sag stormy.
Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army
Attacks once more in ranks on shivering ranks of gray,
But nothing happens.

Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.
Less deadly than the air that shudders black with snow,
With sidelong flowing flakes that flock, pause and renew,
We watch them wandering up and down the wind’s nonchalance,
But nothing happens.
items.passageSource: Wilfred Owen, “Exposure” (written 1917–18), stanzas 1–4
items.hook: The real enemy is the cold: “the merciless iced east winds that knife us”.

items.passage:
(Owen describes soldiers waiting through a freezing night in the trenches in the winter of 1917.)

Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knife us . . .
Wearied we keep awake because the night is silent . . .
Low drooping flares confuse our memory of the salient . . .
Worried by silence, sentries whisper, curious, nervous,
But nothing happens.

Watching, we hear the mad gusts tugging on the wire,
Like twitching agonies of men among its brambles.
Northward incessantly, the flickering gunnery rumbles,
Far off, like a dull rumour of some other war.
What are we doing here?

The poignant misery of dawn begins to grow . . .
We only know war lasts, rain soaks, and clouds sag stormy.
Dawn massing in the east her melancholy army
Attacks once more in ranks on shivering ranks of gray,
But nothing happens.

Sudden successive flights of bullets streak the silence.
Less deadly than the air that shudders black with snow,
With sidelong flowing flakes that flock, pause and renew,
We watch them wandering up and down the wind’s nonchalance,
But nothing happens.

items.prompt: How does Owen present the suffering of soldiers in “Exposure”? Comment on language and structure.
hints: The weather as an enemy (personification)
Sound: sibilance, half-rhyme
Structure: the refrain, the ellipses
What Owen wants his readers at home to understand
items.model: Owen presents suffering that comes not from battle but from cold and waiting. The weather is personified as an attacker: “merciless iced east winds that knife us”, and even dawn arrives like a “melancholy army”. The bullets are “less deadly than the air”, which overturns what readers at home expected war to be. Structurally, the refrain “But nothing happens” closes stanza after stanza, so the poem itself enacts the soldiers’ endless anticlimax, while the trailing ellipses make each line fade like an exhausted mind. Owen’s half-rhymes, such as “silent” and “salient”, never quite resolve, leaving the reader as uneasy as the men.

items.prompt: Compare how Homer and Owen present war. Refer to the Hector extract and “Anthem for Doomed Youth”.
hints: Glory and honour in Homer
Anonymity and waste in Owen
Family and grief in both
Why the writers’ views differ (context)
items.model: Both writers show the cost of war through the people left behind, but they differ in how they view honour. Homer presents war as tragic yet glorious: Hector fights because he would be ashamed to have “shirked battle like a coward”, and prays that his son will be “far better than the father”. Owen, in contrast, sees no glory: his soldiers “die as cattle”, with only “the monstrous anger of the guns” for their funeral. Similarly, both writers turn to grief at home: Andromache weeps even as she smiles, and Owen’s families draw down the blinds. The difference reflects their worlds: Homer sang of heroes for an audience who admired them, whereas Owen wrote from the trenches to shock readers into seeing the truth.
items.passage:
(Two texts about war: Hector’s farewell from the Iliad, then Owen’s “Anthem for Doomed Youth”.)

Hector smiled as he looked upon the boy, but he did not speak, and Andromache stood by him weeping and taking his hand in her own. “Dear husband,” said she, “your valour will bring you to destruction; think on your infant son, and on my hapless self who ere long shall be your widow—for the Achaeans will set upon you in a body and kill you. It would be better for me, should I lose you, to lie dead and buried, for I shall have nothing left to comfort me when you are gone, save only sorrow. I have neither father nor mother now.

[…]

And Hector answered, “Wife, I too have thought upon all this, but with what face should I look upon the Trojans, men or women, if I shirked battle like a coward? I cannot do so: I know nothing save to fight bravely in the forefront of the Trojan host and win renown alike for my father and myself.

[…]

He stretched his arms towards his child, but the boy cried and nestled in his nurse’s bosom, scared at the sight of his father’s armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet. His father and mother laughed to see him, but Hector took the helmet from his head and laid it all gleaming upon the ground. Then he took his darling child, kissed him, and dandled him in his arms, praying over him the while to Jove and to all the gods. “Jove,” he cried, “grant that this my child may be even as myself, chief among the Trojans; let him be not less excellent in strength, and let him rule Ilius with his might. Then may one say of him as he comes from battle, ‘The son is far better than the father.’ May he bring back the blood-stained spoils of him whom he has laid low, and let his mother’s heart be glad.”

With this he laid the child again in the arms of his wife, who took him to her own soft bosom, smiling through her tears.

* * *

What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles’ rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.
No mockeries for them; no prayers nor bells,
Nor any voice of mourning save the choirs,—
The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells;
And bugles calling for them from sad shires.

What candles may be held to speed them all?
Not in the hands of boys, but in their eyes
Shall shine the holy glimmers of goodbyes.
The pallor of girls’ brows shall be their pall;
Their flowers the tenderness of patient minds,
And each slow dusk a drawing-down of blinds.

items.prompt: Compare how Dickens presents Miss Havisham and how Shelley presents the creature. Which is more frightening?
hints: Appearance and contrast in both

A clear judgement
items.model: Both writers frighten us through a body that is wrong. Dickens shows a bride who has “shrunk to skin and bone” inside a dress made for a young woman, while Shelley’s creature has beautiful features that only form “a more horrid contrast” with his watery eyes. In both, the narrator’s reaction guides us: Pip says he “should have cried out”, whereas Victor “rushed out of the room”. However, Miss Havisham is more frightening, because she seems to be a living corpse, with eyes that “moved and looked at me”, while the creature, newly born and abandoned, is already a figure we might pity.
items.passage:
(Two texts: Pip meets Miss Havisham, then Victor Frankenstein sees his creature come to life.)

She was dressed in rich materials,—satins, and lace, and silks,—all of white. Her shoes were white. And she had a long white veil dependent from her hair, and she had bridal flowers in her hair, but her hair was white. Some bright jewels sparkled on her neck and on her hands, and some other jewels lay sparkling on the table. Dresses, less splendid than the dress she wore, and half-packed trunks, were scattered about. She had not quite finished dressing, for she had but one shoe on,—the other was on the table near her hand,—her veil was but half arranged, her watch and chain were not put on, and some lace for her bosom lay with those trinkets, and with her handkerchief, and gloves, and some flowers, and a Prayer-Book all confusedly heaped about the looking-glass.

It was not in the first few moments that I saw all these things, though I saw more of them in the first moments than might be supposed. But I saw that everything within my view which ought to be white, had been white long ago, and had lost its lustre and was faded and yellow. I saw that the bride within the bridal dress had withered like the dress, and like the flowers, and had no brightness left but the brightness of her sunken eyes. I saw that the dress had been put upon the rounded figure of a young woman, and that the figure upon which it now hung loose had shrunk to skin and bone. Once, I had been taken to see some ghastly waxwork at the Fair, representing I know not what impossible personage lying in state. Once, I had been taken to one of our old marsh churches to see a skeleton in the ashes of a rich dress that had been dug out of a vault under the church pavement. Now, waxwork and skeleton seemed to have dark eyes that moved and looked at me. I should have cried out, if I could.

* * *

It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, I collected the instruments of life around me, that I might infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. It was already one in the morning; the rain pattered dismally against the panes, and my candle was nearly burnt out, when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.

How can I describe my emotions at this catastrophe, or how delineate the wretch whom with such infinite pains and care I had endeavoured to form? His limbs were in proportion, and I had selected his features as beautiful. Beautiful! Great God! His yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath; his hair was of a lustrous black, and flowing; his teeth of a pearly whiteness; but these luxuriances only formed a more horrid contrast with his watery eyes, that seemed almost of the same colour as the dun-white sockets in which they were set, his shrivelled complexion and straight black lips.

The different accidents of life are not so changeable as the feelings of human nature. I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body. For this I had deprived myself of rest and health. I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room and continued a long time traversing my bed-chamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep.
items.passageSource: Charles Dickens, Great Expectations (1861); and Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818; revised 1831)
